newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Mahathir tells Australia race row not harming ties.
newsitem.headline: Mahathir tells Australia race row not harming ties.

text.p: Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has reassured Australia that ties between the two nations remain intact despite isolated incidents of racial abuse against young Malaysians studying here.

Mahathir, who warned last month that Malaysia might recall its students from Australia, wrote to an an Australian state premier expressing confidence that local authorities are ensuring the safety of Malaysian students.
"I am glad that the Australians are as concerned about this matter as are Malaysians," Mahathir wrote in the letter released to Reuters in Melbourne on Thursday.
"I do not think these incidents will affect our relations and I am quite sure the government of Victoria will ensure that Malaysian students remain safe."

The letter was released by Victoria Premier Jeff Kennett, who had written to Mahathir after the Malaysian leader warned that thousands of students could be summoned home from Australia's university and school campuses.

Mahathir issued the warning on December 16 after a report that a Malaysian university student, Adrina Shazlin Shukor, was abused for being a foreigner by two Australian men in a car park in the southern city of Melbourne.
Australia has been experiencing its worst immigration backlash in a decade, with migrant and human rights groups reporting a surge in racist sentiment nationwide.
"Thankyou for your letter assuring that what might have happened to Ms Shukor was an isolated incident," Mahathir wrote to Kennett in the December 19 letter.
Of the roughly 53,000 foreigners studying in Australia, over 11,000 are Malaysian.
Australia's universities are concerned about the impact of the race debate on foreign enrolments, which contribute about A$1.3 billion (US$1.03 billion) in annual export earnings.
But the Australian Vice-Chancellors Committee, representing university managements across the country, said on Thursday it was too early to gauge the impact of the row on 1997 enrolments.

"There are some early figures which we've got from somne countries which are down, others are up and some others are stable. It's far too early to tell," committee executive director Stuart Hamilton told Reuters.
The current race row has been sparked by maverick legislator Pauline Hanson's call in September for a freeze on immigration and her warning that Australia risks being "swamped" by Asians.
